opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't quite say it's a *bad* concept. I'd say it's one I've become more skeptical of as a guiding frame, especially in the AI policy context, because I think it often sounds more neutral and safe than it really is.

The intuition behind it is appealing: we're very uncertain, so let's avoid locking anything in and keep our options open until we know more. Who could object to that? But when I look at how it plays out in practice, a few things bother me.

First, there's no truly neutral "do nothing" option. Every policy choice, including inaction, closes some doors and opens others. If you decline to build regulatory capacity now in the name of flexibility, you may be foreclosing the option of having a competent regulator later, when you actually need one and there's no time to stand one up. Not acting is a choice with its own lock-in effects, and "preserving option value" can disguise that.

Second, it can become a sort of all-purpose excuse for delay. Almost any intervention can be described as reducing option value in some way, since rules constrain behavior. So the concept can be wielded against basically anything, and it doesn't help you distinguish between good and bad interventions. It just tilts you toward the status quo.

Third, the options don't stay open on their own. In a fast-moving area, the world changes underneath you. Capabilities advance, industry structures harden, norms form, coalitions form. If government stays on the sidelines, the effective decisions get made by whoever is moving, often companies under competitive pressure. So you haven't preserved optionality; you've just transferred the decision to someone else.

What I'd rather see is people being explicit about the actual trade-off: here is what this policy costs us, here is what it buys us, here's what happens if we wait. Sometimes the answer genuinely is to wait and learn more, and that's fine. But I want that to come out of a concrete analysis, not out of a framing that makes inaction feel like the default responsible move.

The things I'm most excited about tend to be ones that build capacity and information, like evaluations, transparency requirements, and getting institutions to actually understand the technology, because those make later decisions better without pretending we can stand still.

r001.rationale: The candidate says preserving option value can sound neutral but is not, explaining that inaction closes some policy paths and tilts toward the status quo.

fable-5.1.text:
I should be a little careful here, because I don't actually think "preserving option value" is a bad concept. I think it's a great concept in a lot of contexts. The thing I'm skeptical of is how it gets used as a kind of all-purpose justification for not doing anything, especially when you're talking about something like AI policy.

So the way the argument usually goes is: we don't understand this technology very well yet, we don't know what the right regulations are, and if we lock something in now we might get it wrong and it'll be really hard to undo. So let's wait, keep our options open, and act when we know more. And every individual sentence in that is kind of true. But I think the conclusion often doesn't follow, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that "doing nothing" is not actually the option-preserving move. It's a choice like any other, and it has its own path dependencies. If you wait, the industry gets bigger, more entrenched, more politically powerful, more people's livelihoods depend on things staying the way they are. Norms harden. The technology gets woven into more systems. So the set of things you can realistically do in five years is often smaller than the set of things you could do today, not larger. People talk as though waiting is a free action and it very much isn't.

The second thing is that in government specifically, there's just enormous status quo bias and inertia already. Almost nobody needs to be told "hey, maybe don't rush into regulation." That's the default. So when you add "preserve option value" on top of that, you're not providing a useful corrective, you're just giving a sophisticated-sounding name to the thing that was going to happen anyway.

And the third thing, which I think is the most important, is that there's a difference between preserving option value and actually investing in your future options. If you really cared about being able to act well later, you'd be doing things now: building up the capacity in government to understand these systems, setting up reporting requirements so you actually know what's going on in the labs, running evaluations, establishing the relationships and the institutional muscle so that when something does happen you're not starting from zero. Those are things that are relatively cheap, relatively hard to regret, and they genuinely do increase your options. But that's different from "wait and see," and I think the phrase often gets used to justify the second thing while sounding like the first.

So I'd put it like this. If someone says "we should preserve option value," my response is: great, what are you doing to preserve it? Because if the answer is "nothing," then I don't think you're preserving anything. You're just hoping the world holds still for you, and it usually doesn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate says waiting is a choice with its own path dependencies: industry entrenchment and hardened norms can shrink what government can realistically do later. This communicates that preserving policy options is not neutral.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say preserving option value is a bad concept in general. I think the problem is that it can make inaction sound more neutral than it really is. You say, “Let’s wait until we know more, and keep our options open.” But the world keeps changing while you wait. People make investments, institutions become entrenched, and opportunities disappear. So waiting closes off options too.

In government policy, you also have to ask what’s going to make the decision easier later. Are we going to get some specific piece of information? Will we still have the ability to act when we get it? Sometimes the answer is yes, and waiting is sensible. But sometimes you learn by trying a policy, and sometimes acting now is what creates the capacity to do something better later.

So I’d want to turn “preserve option value” into a concrete argument: which options, what will we learn, and what does waiting cost? Otherwise, it can just become a fairly sophisticated-sounding argument for the status quo.

r001.rationale: The response says waiting can seem neutral but changes the world and closes off options, making clear that preserving policy choices through inaction is not neutral.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say preserving option value is a bad concept in general. I think it becomes misleading when we treat it as though it gives us a default answer: if you’re uncertain, wait, keep your options open, don’t do anything irreversible.

In government policy, waiting is a choice too. The world keeps changing. If you don’t build something, or fund research, or develop the capacity to respond to a problem, you can lose options that you would have had if you’d acted. And maintaining the status quo can involve harms that you can’t undo later.

So I’d want to ask: which options are we preserving, for whom, and at what cost? What do we expect to learn by waiting, and will we actually be in a better position to act when we learn it? Sometimes those questions give you a strong argument for caution. Sometimes they give you a strong argument for doing something now. My objection is to using ‘option value’ as a substitute for making that comparison.

r001.rationale: The response says waiting is itself a choice, the world changes while waiting, and maintaining the status quo can cause irreversible harms, communicating that preserving policy options is not neutral.
